title: Prelude
paragraphs: Who, if they care deeply about human history and the behaviour of that mysterious mixture under Time’s changing experiments, has not paused, at least briefly, over the life of Saint Theresa? Who has not smiled tenderly at the thought of the little girl setting off one morning, hand in hand with her even smaller brother, to seek martyrdom in the land of the Moors? They toddled out of rugged Avila, as wide-eyed and apparently helpless as two fawns, yet with human hearts already beating to a national ideal, until the realities of home, in the shape of their uncles, intercepted them and turned them back from their great purpose. That childhood pilgrimage was a fitting beginning. Theresa’s passionate, idealistic nature demanded an epic life: what could the many volumes of chivalric romances, or a brilliant girl’s triumphs in society, mean to her? Her fire soon consumed such flimsy fuel. Sustained from within, it rose towards some boundless satisfaction, some purpose that could never excuse weariness, that would reconcile despair of herself with the ecstatic awareness of a life beyond herself. She found her epic in reforming a religious order.

That Spanish woman, who lived three hundred years ago, was certainly not the last of her kind. Many Theresas have been born without finding an epic life in which great actions unfolded continuously and sent their echoes far away. They may have found only a life of mistakes, born of a certain greatness of spirit poorly matched with the smallness of their opportunities; perhaps a tragic failure that found no sacred poet and slipped, unmourned, into oblivion. With little light to guide them and circumstances tangled around them, they tried to bring their thoughts and actions into noble harmony. Yet to ordinary eyes their struggles seemed nothing but inconsistency and shapelessness. These later Theresas had no coherent social faith or order to supply the place of knowledge for the soul passionately willing to act. Their fervour shifted between a vague ideal and the ordinary longings of womanhood: the first was censured as extravagance, the second condemned as a falling away.

Some have thought these stumbling lives the result of the inconvenient lack of definition with which the Supreme Power has made women’s natures. If female incompetence had one fixed level, as definite as the ability to count to three and no further, women’s place in society could be settled with scientific certainty. The indefiniteness persists, however, and the actual range of variation is far wider than anyone would guess from the uniformity of women’s hairstyles and their favourite love stories in prose and verse. Here and there a young swan grows up uneasily among the ducklings in a brown pond and never finds the flowing stream and the company of its own paddle-footed kind. Here and there a Saint Theresa is born who founds nothing, whose loving heartbeats and sobs for a goodness never reached tremble away and scatter among obstacles, instead of gathering into some deed that people will recognize long afterwards.
